title: Adolescent smartphone use, sleep, and physical activity: daily associations between sensor-based measures in the adolescent brain cognitive development (ABCD) study
authors: Alexander JD, Nguyen-Louie TT, Gupta S, Cummins KM, Wade NE

primary_models.name: Linear mixed-effects regression of daily Fitbit sleep and physical activity outcomes on same-day passively sensed smartphone app or keyboard minutes (combined effect), adjusted for sex, age, day type, summer, Fitbit wear time
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 3 'Combined Effect' columns (p. 6); Results p. 4; Abstract; Discussion pp. 6 and 8.
primary_models.design: Intensive longitudinal (daily diary-style) design within the ABCD Year-4 follow-up: up to three weeks of daily passive sensor data per participant. IV and DV are measured on the same day (activity outcomes), the same night (sleep onset, total sleep) or the next morning (wake time). Days are repeated measures nested within participants, handled by a participant random intercept. The combined effect uses raw daily minutes of use, so it does not separate within-person from between-person variation. No time trend or IV x time interaction.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1, Year-4 follow-up visit (ages 13-14), participants in the ABCD EARS/Fitbit wearables substudy who concurrently provided up to three weeks of passively sensed smartphone, sleep and physical activity data (data collection ended after 21 days of data or 42 elapsed days). N = 791 participants overall (Table 1): mean age 14.12 (SD 0.69); 369 male (46.6%), 422 female (53.4%); Asian 17 (2.1%), Black 75 (9.5%), Hispanic 144 (18.2%), White 471 (59.5%), another race 84 (10.6%); highest parent education: no HS diploma 15 (1.8%), HS/GED 40 (5.1%), some college 241 (30.5%), bachelor's 225 (28.4%), graduate/professional 270 (34.1%); iOS 486 (61.4%), Android 305 (38.6%). Keyboard measures come from all 791 participants (11,797 day-observations for daytime and evening, 10,159 for late night); application-use measures come only from Android users (302 participants, 6340 days; 5993 for late night). Fitbit outcomes: steps 791 participants / 6228 days; sedentary and exercise 791 / 6748 days; total sleep and sleep onset 604 / 5634 nights; wake time 604 / 5375 nights (Table 2). The paper reports 6748 days of concurrent smartphone and physical activity data and 5634 nights of concurrent smartphone and sleep data. Each model uses all pairwise-complete day-observations for that IV-DV pair; the exact day-level and participant-level N per model is not reported. Attrition and inclusion detail is in Supplementary Figure S1 (not in this PDF). The authors note the sample is more female and more non-Hispanic White and less low-income than the US population of 10-14 year olds.
primary_models.iv: Passively sensed smartphone use from the EARS app. Application use (Android only) is the minutes any application, third-party or native, was in the foreground each day, after removing system apps and apps meant to stay foregrounded during sleep (lock screens, alarm clocks). Keyboard use (Android and iOS) is the total minutes the keyboard was open and logging keystrokes (time between first and last keystroke of each session), with the same app exclusions; on Android it was recorded from the native keyboard, on iOS via an EARS keyboard overlay that participants were told to use exclusively. Each is split into three time windows: daytime/evening 6:00AM-7:59PM, 'night time' 8:00PM-9:59PM, and late night 10:00PM-5:59AM the next morning. Six IVs total, each entered in a separate model, in minutes. Table 2 descriptives: Smartphone application use, 6:00AM-7:59PM (min/day): grand M = 190.47 min, SD = 140.26; participant-mean M = 188.68, SD = 96.00; Smartphone application use, 8:00PM-9:59PM (min/day): grand M = 37.66 min, SD = 36.89; participant-mean M = 36.98, SD = 23.10; Smartphone application use, 10:00PM-5:59AM (min/night): grand M = 71.52 min, SD = 97.11; participant-mean M = 70.53, SD = 69.58; Keyboard use, 6:00AM-7:59PM (min/day): grand M = 11.68 min, SD = 21.28; participant-mean M = 9.89, SD = 14.62; Keyboard use, 8:00PM-9:59PM (min/day): grand M = 2.90 min, SD = 7.27; participant-mean M = 2.47, SD = 4.52; Keyboard use, 10:00PM-5:59AM (min/night): grand M = 4.04 min, SD = 12.25; participant-mean M = 3.33, SD = 7.68.
primary_models.dv: Six Fitbit Charge-derived daily outcomes, each modeled separately: total daily steps (grand M = 7553.73, SD = 4578.02); minutes of sedentary activity (METs < 1.5; M = 973.01, SD = 333.41); minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise (METs >= 3.0; M = 31.73, SD = 47.52); total minutes of sleep between 5:00PM and 4:59PM the next day (M = 449.98, SD = 95.39); sleep onset, first minute recorded asleep each night, modeled as minutes delayed (grand M = 11:48PM, SD = 2 h 14 m; labeled 'Bedtime' in Table 3); wake time, first minute awake followed by at least 30 consecutive minutes awake, modeled as minutes delayed (grand M = 8:02AM, SD = 2 h 17 m). Physical-activity outcomes are same-day; sleep onset and total sleep are same-night; wake time is next morning. Days with < 599 min of valid waking wear, > 20% of steps excluded in QC, or < 30 s of recorded sleep were excluded. Grand means/SDs from Table 2 (p. 5).

primary_models.equation: Outcome[i,t] = b0 + b1*PhoneUse_minutes[i,t] + b2*sex[i] + b3*age_c[i] + b4*weekend[t] + b5*school_night[t] + b6*summer[t] + b7*fitbit_wear[i,t] (+ b8*OS[i] in keyboard models) + u_i + e[i,t]; one model per PhoneUse measure (6) x Outcome (6). Covariate set 'varied by model' per the Table 3 note.
primary_models.estimation: Linear mixed-effects models fit with the nlme package in R 4.3.0, with individual-level random intercepts. A separate model was fit for every smartphone measure x outcome pair. Table 3 reports both the unstandardized beta (per additional minute of use) and the standardized beta; no CIs or SEs are printed in the table, though Fig. 1 plots 95% CIs for the within- and between-person standardized betas. Significance judged at P < .05 (Fig. 1 marks * P < .05); no multiple-comparison correction is reported across the 36 combined or 72 disaggregated tests. No interaction or stratified analyses by sex or other demographics. Sensitivity analyses reported only in the supplement (not in this PDF) and summarized narratively on p. 5: adding race and socioeconomic status (all significant effects retained), adding time recorded awake to the physical activity models (11/15 retained), redefining late night as 9:00PM-4:59AM or 11:00PM-6:59AM, winsorizing outcomes at +/-3 SD (30/31 retained), and inverse-propensity weighting by proportion of complete days (25/31 retained). Standardized effects in all sensitivity models were within 0.10 SD of the primary effects.

primary_models.name: Linear mixed-effects regression of daily Fitbit sleep and physical activity outcomes on within-person (person-mean-centered) and between-person (person-mean) smartphone app or keyboard minutes, same covariates as M1
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 3 'Within-Person Effect' and 'Between-Person Effect' columns (p. 6); Fig. 1 (p. 7, standardized betas with 95% CIs); Results pp. 4-5; Abstract; Discussion p. 8.
primary_models.design: Same intensive longitudinal Year-4 data as M1. Each smartphone measure is decomposed into a between-person term (the participant's mean daily use over the study) and a within-person term (that day's use minus the participant's mean). Both terms enter the same model as fixed effects, so the within-person coefficient estimates the association of a day of above-usual use with that day's/night's outcome, net of stable individual differences in use. Repeated days nested in participants with a random intercept.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1, Year-4 follow-up visit (ages 13-14), participants in the ABCD EARS/Fitbit wearables substudy who concurrently provided up to three weeks of passively sensed smartphone, sleep and physical activity data (data collection ended after 21 days of data or 42 elapsed days). Keyboard measures come from all 791 participants (11,797 day-observations for daytime and evening, 10,159 for late night); application-use measures come only from Android users (302 participants, 6340 days; 5993 for late night). Fitbit outcomes: steps 791 participants / 6228 days; sedentary and exercise 791 / 6748 days; total sleep and sleep onset 604 / 5634 nights; wake time 604 / 5375 nights (Table 2). The paper reports 6748 days of concurrent smartphone and physical activity data and 5634 nights of concurrent smartphone and sleep data. primary_models.iv: Same six smartphone measures as M1, each decomposed into two terms: between-person (participant mean minutes) and within-person (daily minutes minus participant mean). Participant-mean SDs from Table 2: app 6:00AM-7:59PM 96.00; app 8:00PM-9:59PM 23.10; app 10:00PM-5:59AM 69.58; keyboard 6:00AM-7:59PM 14.62; keyboard 8:00PM-9:59PM 4.52; keyboard 10:00PM-5:59AM 7.68. The SD of the within-person deviation is not reported.
primary_models.dv: Same six Fitbit outcomes as M1.

excluded_models.model: Hourly-binned smartphone application use relative to sleep onset (12 h before to 12+ h after) predicting sleep duration and step count
excluded_models.location: Supplementary Figure S1 (not in this PDF); summarized in Results pp. 5-6
excluded_models.why: Per-bin estimates are not printed in the paper; the text gives only ranges of unstandardized betas and p-values across bins (e.g., sleep duration beta range -91.73 to -17.02 s for post-onset bins). No single cell-level estimate with its own location is extractable from the article PDF.

excluded_models.model: Sensitivity models (adding race and SES; adding time awake to activity models; late-night redefined as 9:00PM-4:59AM and 11:00PM-6:59AM; winsorized outcomes +/-3 SD; inverse-propensity weighting for missing data)
excluded_models.location: Supplementary material (not in this PDF); summarized narratively p. 5
excluded_models.why: Only counts of retained significant effects and the statement that standardized effects were within 0.10 SD of primary effects are given; no per-cell numbers in the article.

excluded_models.model: Smartphone operating system (iOS vs. Android) as a fixed-effect covariate in keyboard models
excluded_models.why: OS is a covariate, not the focal smartphone use variable; its coefficients (standardized beta 0.09-0.18 for steps/exercise, -0.17 to -0.16 for sedentary) describe device platform differences, not amount of smartphone use.

excluded_models.model: Covariate effects in full model outputs
excluded_models.why: Non-phone covariate coefficients; not in this PDF and not phone/SM estimates.

d_transformation.native_metric: beta_std (standardized beta from linear mixed models; unstandardized B per minute also printed)
d_transformation.conversion_formula: Standardized beta treated as approximate r: d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (guidelines section 4a). Alternative from raw B: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV, then the same formula.
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 SD of daily minutes of smartphone app or keyboard use in the given time window (combined effect, M1); per 1 SD of the within-person daily deviation (M2 within) or of the participant mean (M2 between)
d_transformation.notes: The paper prints standardized betas directly in Table 3 (p. 6), so d can be derived without SDs. No CIs or SEs are printed in the table, so d CIs cannot be computed from the table; Fig. 1 (p. 7) plots 95% CIs for M2 betas but these were not read off the figure. sd_iv for M1 is the grand (all-observation) SD from Table 2 (p. 5); sd_iv for M2 between-person terms is the participant-mean SD from Table 2; the within-person deviation SD is not reported (null). sd_dv is the grand SD from Table 2: steps 4578.02, sedentary 333.41, exercise 47.52, total sleep 95.39; sleep onset SD printed as '2 h, 14 m' and wake time as '2 h, 17 m', converted to 134 and 137 min. The paper does not state exactly how beta_std was standardized (e.g., grand vs. within SDs); recomputing B*SD_IV/SD_DV with the grand SDs reproduces the printed beta_std only approximately (e.g., app 6AM-7:59PM on exercise: -0.046*140.26/47.52 = -0.136 vs. printed -0.128), so the printed beta_std should be used. Effects are per-day associations from intensive longitudinal data and are not directly comparable to between-person cross-sectional d's from questionnaire-based papers.

extraction_flags: 1) The authors interpret both the combined-effect models and the within/between decomposition (both appear in the Abstract), so I extracted two cards: M1 with 36 combined estimates and M2 with 72 within- and between-person estimates. A reviewer should decide whether both cards belong in the meta-matrix or only one; they share the same data. 2) Native metric is set to the standardized beta printed in Table 3. Each estimate's note gives the unstandardized B per minute. No CIs or SEs are printed in Table 3. Fig. 1 plots 95% CIs for the M2 betas, but I did not read values off the figure, so beta_lo and beta_hi are null. 3) The paper does not say how beta_std was standardized.
